statement: Let $f, g$ be [integrable functions](c:integrable-function) on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). Then $f * g$ converges absolutely almost everywhere, is integrable with $\|f * g\|_1 \le \|f\|_1 \|g\|_1$, and satisfies $f * g = g * f$ almost everywhere. Also $\mathcal{F}(f * g)(\xi) = \mathcal{F}f(\xi)\,\mathcal{F}g(\xi)$ for every $\xi$.

hypotheses.text: The functions $f$ and $g$ are measurable and [integrable](c:integrable-function): $\int |f| < \infty$ and $\int |g| < \infty$.
The measure is [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure), which is invariant under translation and under $x \mapsto -x$.

conclusion: The [convolution](c:convolution) $f * g$ is defined almost everywhere, is integrable with norm at most $\|f\|_1\|g\|_1$, is commutative, and has [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) $\mathcal{F}f \cdot \mathcal{F}g$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the product rule, for integrable functions with values in a normed algebra. Integrability and commutativity of the convolution are separate facts.

proofs.name: Tonelli bound, then a Fubini swap
proofs.slogan: Bound the double integral of absolute values by Tonelli, then swap the integrals and factor the exponential.
proofs.scope: The whole statement under all listed hypotheses.

roles.why: Finite norms make the double integral of absolute values finite.
Invariance of the measure under shears and translations keeps measurability and the norms.
Complex values let the exponential factor split the transform.

steps.slogan: Show that the integrand $f(y)g(x-y)$ is measurable on the product space.
steps.detail: The map $(x,y) \mapsto (y, x-y)$ is a linear bijection of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with determinant $\pm 1$. It preserves Lebesgue measure. So $(x,y) \mapsto f(y)g(x-y)$ is measurable.

steps.slogan: Bound the double integral of the absolute values with Tonelli's theorem.
steps.detail: By Tonelli, $\iint |f(y)||g(x-y)|\,dy\,dx = \int |f(y)| \big(\int |g(x-y)|\,dx\big)dy$. Translation invariance gives $\int |g(x-y)|\,dx = \|g\|_1$. So the double integral equals $\|f\|_1\|g\|_1 < \infty$.

steps.slogan: Read the existence and the norm bound from the finite double integral.
steps.detail: A finite double integral makes the inner integral finite for almost every $x$. Also $|(f*g)(x)| \le \int |f(y)||g(x-y)|\,dy$, and integration in $x$ gives $\|f*g\|_1 \le \|f\|_1\|g\|_1$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $y \mapsto x-y$ to prove that the convolution is commutative.
steps.detail: The substitution preserves Lebesgue measure. So $\int f(y)g(x-y)\,dy = \int f(x-y)g(y)\,dy$ at each $x$ where one side converges absolutely.

steps.slogan: Swap the two integrals in the Fourier transform of the convolution with Fubini's theorem.
steps.detail: Fix $\xi$. The integrand of $\mathcal{F}(f*g)(\xi)$ has absolute value $|f(y)||g(x-y)|$, which is integrable on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ by the Tonelli bound. So Fubini gives $\int f(y)\big(\int g(x-y)e^{-2\pi i\langle x,\xi\rangle}dx\big)dy$.

steps.slogan: Factor the exponential in the inner integral to split the product of transforms.
steps.detail: Put $x = y + w$. Then $e^{-2\pi i\langle y+w,\xi\rangle} = e^{-2\pi i\langle y,\xi\rangle}e^{-2\pi i\langle w,\xi\rangle}$, so the inner integral is $e^{-2\pi i\langle y,\xi\rangle}\mathcal{F}g(\xi)$. The outer integral then gives $\mathcal{F}f(\xi)\,\mathcal{F}g(\xi)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the four parts of the statement from the earlier steps.
steps.detail: The steps give absolute convergence and integrability with the norm bound, commutativity, and the product rule for the transform at every $\xi$.

concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability of both functions makes the double integral finite.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Invariance of the measure supports the shear, the translation and the substitution.
concepts.c:convolution: The proof studies the integral that defines $f * g$.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The product rule is the claim about the transform of the convolution.

statement: Let $1 \le p, q, r < \infty$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1 + 1/r$. Let $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then $\int |f(y)||g(x-y)|\,dy$ is finite for almost every $x$, the [convolution](c:convolution) $f * g$ lies in $L^r$, and $\|f * g\|_r \le \|f\|_p \|g\|_q$.

hypotheses.text: The exponents satisfy $1 \le p, q, r < \infty$ and $1/p + 1/q = 1 + 1/r$, which forces $p \le r$ and $q \le r$.
The function $f$ is in $L^p$ and the function $g$ is in $L^q$.

conclusion: The function $f * g$ is defined almost everywhere, lies in $L^r$, and has [norm](c:norm) at most $\|f\|_p \|g\|_q$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the pointwise Holder bound for the integrand, for a Holder triple of exponents. It is a smaller fact that step 4 uses, not the Young inequality.

proofs.name: Three-exponent Holder splitting
proofs.slogan: Split the integrand into three factors, apply Holder with three exponents, then integrate in $x$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The constant 1 is not claimed to be sharp.

roles.why: Translation invariance turns the integral of $G(x-y)^q$ in $x$ into $\|G\|_q^q$.
The relation between the exponents defines $s, t$ and makes the final powers equal $r$.
Finite $L^p$ and $L^q$ norms bound the three integrals that Holder produces.

steps.slogan: Define the exponents $s$ and $t$ and check that $1/r + 1/s + 1/t = 1$.
steps.detail: Put $1/s = 1/p - 1/r$ and $1/t = 1/q - 1/r$. From $1/p = 1 + 1/r - 1/q \ge 1/r$ we get $1/s \ge 0$, and likewise $1/t \ge 0$. Also $1/r + 1/s + 1/t = 1/p + 1/q - 1/r = 1$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to nonnegative functions by the bound $|f*g| \le |f|*|g|$.
steps.detail: Since $|f * g| \le |f| * |g|$, it is enough to treat $F = |f|$ and $G = |g|$.

steps.slogan: Split the integrand $F(y)G(x-y)$ into three factors with exponents $r, s, t$.
steps.detail: Write $F(y)G(x-y) = [F(y)^p G(x-y)^q]^{1/r} \cdot F(y)^{p/s} \cdot G(x-y)^{q/t}$. The exponent of $F$ is $p/r + p/s = p \cdot (1/p) = 1$, and the exponent of $G$ is checked in the same way. If $1/s = 0$, the factor $F^{p/s}$ is 1.

steps.slogan: Apply the three-exponent [Holder inequality](c:holder-triple) with exponents $r, s, t$ at fixed $x$.
steps.detail: This gives $(F*G)(x) \le \big(\int F(y)^p G(x-y)^q\,dy\big)^{1/r} \big(\int F^p\big)^{1/s} \big(\int G^q\big)^{1/t}$. Here $(F^{p/s})^s = F^p$, and the same holds for $G$.

steps.slogan: Raise the bound to the power $r$ and integrate in $x$ with Tonelli's theorem.
steps.detail: By Tonelli and translation invariance, $\iint F(y)^p G(x-y)^q\,dy\,dx = \|F\|_p^p \|G\|_q^q$. Hence $\|F*G\|_r^r \le \|F\|_p^p \|G\|_q^q \cdot \|F\|_p^{pr/s} \|G\|_q^{qr/t}$.

steps.slogan: Count the exponents of the two norms and take the $r$-th root.
steps.detail: The power of $\|F\|_p$ is $p + pr/s = p(1 + r(1/p - 1/r)) = r$, and the power of $\|G\|_q$ is $r$ in the same way. So $\|F*G\|_r^r \le (\|F\|_p\|G\|_q)^r$. A finite norm makes $F*G(x)$ finite almost everywhere.

concepts.c:convolution: The proof bounds the integral that defines $f * g$.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Translation invariance of the measure evaluates the integral in $x$.
concepts.c:norm: The claim bounds one norm by a product of two norms.
concepts.c:lp-space: The hypotheses put $f$ and $g$ in $L^p$ spaces with finite norms.
concepts.c:holder-triple: Holder with three exponents is the main estimate of the proof.

statement: Let $u$ be a real [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) near the closed disc $\bar B(c,R)$ with $u \ge 0$ on the circle $|z-c|=R$. Let $|w-c| = \rho < R$. Then $\frac{R-\rho}{R+\rho}\,u(c) \le u(w) \le \frac{R+\rho}{R-\rho}\,u(c)$. If $u \ge 0$ is harmonic on all of $\mathbb{C}$, then $u$ is constant.

hypotheses.text: The function $u$ is real valued and [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) on a neighbourhood of the closed disc.
The function $u$ is nonnegative on the circle $|z-c|=R$.
For the second claim, $u$ is harmonic and nonnegative on all of $\mathbb{C}$.

conclusion: The two-sided Harnack bound holds at $w$, and a nonnegative harmonic function on $\mathbb{C}$ is constant.

formal.difference: The declaration states the upper bound for the real part of the Herglotz-Riesz kernel on the circle. It is a smaller fact that gives the kernel bound of step 3.

proofs.name: Poisson kernel bounds
proofs.slogan: Write $u(w)$ as a Poisson integral, bound the kernel on both sides, and let the radius grow for Liouville.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The disc inequality uses steps 1 to 5; the Liouville claim uses step 6 as well.

roles.why: Harmonicity gives the Poisson formula and the mean value property.
Nonnegativity on the circle lets the kernel bounds pass to $u$.
The distance $\rho < R$ keeps the kernel positive and bounded.
Harmonicity and nonnegativity on $\mathbb{C}$ allow every radius $R$.

steps.slogan: Write $u(w)$ as the Poisson integral of its values on the circle.
steps.detail: For $u$ harmonic near the closed disc, $u(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} u(c + Re^{i\theta})\,P(\theta)\,d\theta$, where $P$ is the real part of the Herglotz-Riesz kernel.

steps.slogan: Compute the closed form of the [Poisson kernel](c:poisson-kernel) $P(\theta)$.
steps.detail: Put $\zeta = Re^{i\theta}$ and $\eta = w-c$. Then $\mathrm{Re}\big((\zeta+\eta)(\bar\zeta-\bar\eta)\big) = |\zeta|^2 - |\eta|^2 + \mathrm{Re}(\eta\bar\zeta - \zeta\bar\eta)$. The last term is purely imaginary, so $P(\theta) = (R^2-\rho^2)/|\zeta-\eta|^2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the kernel above and below with the triangle inequality.
steps.detail: The triangle inequality gives $R-\rho \le |\zeta-\eta| \le R+\rho$. So $\frac{R-\rho}{R+\rho} \le P(\theta) \le \frac{R+\rho}{R-\rho}$ for all $\theta$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the kernel bounds by the nonnegative values of $u$ on the circle.
steps.detail: Since $u \ge 0$ on the circle, the inequalities survive the multiplication and the integration. So $\frac{R-\rho}{R+\rho}\,\mathrm{avg}(u) \le u(w) \le \frac{R+\rho}{R-\rho}\,\mathrm{avg}(u)$, where $\mathrm{avg}(u)$ is the circle average.

steps.slogan: Replace the circle average by $u(c)$ with the mean value property.
steps.detail: For harmonic $u$, the circle average equals $u(c)$. Put this in the two-sided bound to get the Harnack inequality.

steps.slogan: Let $R$ tend to infinity to prove that a nonnegative entire harmonic function is constant.
steps.detail: Fix $c$ and $w$. For every $R > |w-c|$ the Harnack inequality holds. As $R \to \infty$, both ratios $\frac{R-\rho}{R+\rho}$ and $\frac{R+\rho}{R-\rho}$ tend to 1, so $u(w) = u(c)$. Hence $u$ is constant.

concepts.c:harmonic-function: Harmonicity gives the integral representation and the mean value property.
concepts.c:poisson-kernel: Bounds on the kernel give the two sides of the Harnack inequality.

statement: For $t > 0$ put $G_t(x) = (4\pi t)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/(4t)}$. Then $\mathcal{F}G_t(\xi) = e^{-4\pi^2 t\xi^2}$ and $G_s * G_t = G_{s+t}$. For an [integrable function](c:integrable-function) $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the function $u = G_t * f$ is smooth, solves $u_t = u_{xx}$, and has $\mathcal{F}u(t,\cdot) = e^{-4\pi^2 t\xi^2}\mathcal{F}f$, $\|u(t,\cdot)\|_1 \le \|f\|_1$ and $\int u = \int f$.
conclusion: The [heat kernel](c:heat-kernel) has the stated [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) and semigroup law, and $u = G_t * f$ solves the [heat equation](c:heat-equation) with the stated transform, norm bound and total mass.

formal.difference: The declaration states the transform of the Gaussian $e^{-\pi b x^2}$ only. It gives part (i) after scaling; the other parts are separate facts.

proofs.name: Gaussian transform and differentiation under the integral
proofs.slogan: Find the transform of the Gaussian by an ODE, scale it, then differentiate the convolution under the integral.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The entry does not prove that $u(t,\cdot)$ tends to $f$ as $t \to 0$, and it does not prove uniqueness.

roles.why: Integrability of $f$ bounds the differentiated integrand and gives the norm and mass identities.
A positive time makes $G_t$ defined, positive and smooth.

steps.slogan: Find the transform $e^{-\pi\xi^2}$ of the standard Gaussian with a differential equation.
steps.detail: Let $H(\xi) = \int e^{-\pi x^2}e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$. Since $-2\pi i x\,e^{-\pi x^2} = i\,(e^{-\pi x^2})'$, integration by parts gives $H'(\xi) = -2\pi\xi H(\xi)$. With $H(0) = 1$ this gives $H(\xi) = e^{-\pi\xi^2}$.

steps.slogan: Scale the standard Gaussian to get the transform of $G_t$.
steps.detail: Let $a = (4\pi t)^{-1/2}$. Then $G_t(x) = a\,e^{-\pi(ax)^2}$, and dilation gives $\mathcal{F}G_t(\xi) = H(\xi/a) = e^{-4\pi^2 t\xi^2}$. This is part (i).

steps.slogan: Add the variances of the two normal laws to prove the semigroup law.
steps.detail: The function $G_t$ is the density of a normal law with variance $2t$. The convolution of normal laws adds variances, so $G_s * G_t$ has variance $2(s+t)$ and equals $G_{s+t}$.

steps.slogan: Check by direct differentiation that the kernel solves the heat equation.
steps.detail: We have $\partial_x G_t = -\frac{x}{2t}G_t$, so $\partial_x^2 G_t = \big(-\frac{1}{2t} + \frac{x^2}{4t^2}\big)G_t$. The same factor gives $\partial_t G_t$. So $\partial_t G_t = \partial_x^2 G_t$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate under the integral sign with a bound that does not depend on $x$.
steps.detail: For $t \in [a,b] \subset (0,\infty)$, every derivative of $G_t(z)$ in $(t,z)$ is bounded by a constant $C$. So $|f(y)\,\partial G_t(x-y)| \le C|f(y)|$, which is integrable. Dominated convergence shows that $u$ is smooth and $u_t = f * \partial_t G_t = f * \partial_x^2 G_t = u_{xx}$.

steps.slogan: Take the transform, the norm and the mass of $u$ from the convolution theorem.
steps.detail: The convolution theorem for $L^1$ gives $\mathcal{F}u(t) = \mathcal{F}G_t \cdot \mathcal{F}f$. Since $G_t > 0$ and $\int G_t = 1$, we get $\|u(t)\|_1 \le \|f\|_1\|G_t\|_1 = \|f\|_1$ and $\int u = \int f \int G_t = \int f$.

steps.slogan: Collect the kernel and solution properties into the statement.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give parts (i) and (ii). Steps 5 and 6 give smoothness, the equation, the transform, the norm bound and the mass.

concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability bounds the differentiated integrand and gives the norm and mass identities.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The transform turns the Gaussian into a Gaussian and the convolution into a product.
concepts.c:heat-kernel: The Gaussian $G_t$ is the kernel whose convolution solves the equation.
concepts.c:heat-equation: The equation $u_t = u_{xx}$ is the claim that the convolution satisfies.

statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be [finite](c:finite-measure) [Borel measures](c:borel-measure) on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Put $\hat\mu(t) = \int e^{i\langle x,tangle}d\mu(x)$. If $\hat\mu = \hat
u$ everywhere, then $\mu = 
u$. For the convolution of finite measures, $\widehat{\mu*
u}(t) = \hat\mu(t)\hat
u(t)$.

hypotheses.text: The measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ are [finite](c:finite-measure) Borel measures.
The space is $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the Euclidean inner product.

conclusion: The measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ are equal, and the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of a convolution is the product of the characteristic functions.

formal.difference: The declaration states part (i) only, for finite measures on a complete second-countable inner product space. Part (ii) is a separate fact.

proofs.name: Gaussian smoothing
proofs.slogan: Smooth both measures with a Gaussian, show that the smoothings agree, then let the width shrink to recover the measures.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. Part (i) uses steps 1 to 4; part (ii) uses step 5.

roles.why: Finite mass bounds the smoothed integrals and allows Fubini and dominated convergence.
The inner product defines the characters and the Gaussian kernel.
Equal characteristic functions make the two smoothings equal.

steps.slogan: Smooth the measure $\mu$ with a Gaussian and write the result through $\hat\mu$.
steps.detail: For $\varepsilon > 0$ the Gaussian identity (see the [Gaussian integral](c:gaussian-integral)) gives $e^{-\varepsilon^2|z|^2/2} = (2\pi)^{-d/2}\varepsilon^{-d}\int e^{i\langle z,t\rangle}e^{-|t|^2/(2\varepsilon^2)}dt$. Put $z = x-y$ and integrate in $\mu$. The integrand is bounded by $e^{-|t|^2/(2\varepsilon^2)}$ times the finite mass, so Fubini gives $\int e^{-\varepsilon^2|x-y|^2/2}d\mu(x) = (2\pi)^{-d/2}\varepsilon^{-d}\int e^{-|t|^2/(2\varepsilon^2)}e^{-i\langle y,t\rangle}\hat\mu(t)\,dt$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the two smoothed integrals agree for every point and every width.
steps.detail: The right side depends on $\mu$ only through $\hat\mu$. So if $\hat\mu = \hat\nu$, then $\int k_\varepsilon(x-y)\,d\mu(x) = \int k_\varepsilon(x-y)\,d\nu(x)$ for every $y$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, where $k_\varepsilon$ is the Gaussian kernel.

steps.slogan: Integrate against a compactly supported continuous function and let the width shrink.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi$ be continuous with compact support. Fubini and the evenness of $k_\varepsilon$ give $\int (k_\varepsilon * \varphi)\,d\mu = \int (k_\varepsilon * \varphi)\,d\nu$. As the kernel concentrates, $k_\varepsilon * \varphi \to \varphi$ uniformly, with bound $\sup|\varphi|$. Dominated convergence gives $\int\varphi\,d\mu = \int\varphi\,d\nu$.

steps.slogan: Identify the measures from their integrals of compactly supported continuous functions.
steps.detail: Two finite Borel measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$ that agree on all continuous functions of compact support are equal, by uniqueness in the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani representation. So $\mu = \nu$.

steps.slogan: Split the double integral of the convolution into a product by Fubini's theorem.
steps.detail:
We have $\widehat{\mu*
u}(t) = \iint e^{i\langle x+y,tangle}d\mu(x)\,d
u(y)$. The integrand has modulus 1 and the measures are finite, so Fubini applies and the integral splits into $\hat\mu(t)\hat
u(t)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the uniqueness claim and the product rule as the conclusion.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives $\mu = \nu$ from equal characteristic functions. Step 5 gives the product rule for the convolution.

concepts.c:finite-measure: Finite mass makes the smoothed integrals converge and allows Fubini.
concepts.c:borel-measure: Borel measures are the objects that integrals of continuous functions determine.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: The transform $\hat\mu$ carries all information about $\mu$.
concepts.c:gaussian-integral: The Gaussian integral supplies the identity that smooths the measure.

statement: Let $T$ be a complex [matrix](c:matrix) with finite index sets $J$ (columns) and $I$ (rows). Let $1 \le p_0, p_1 < \infty$ and $1 < q_0, q_1 < \infty$. Let $M_i$ be the [operator norm](c:operator-norm) of $T$ from $\ell^{p_i}(J)$ to $\ell^{q_i}(I)$. For $0 < t < 1$, define $p, q$ by $1/p = (1-t)/p_0 + t/p_1$ and $1/q = (1-t)/q_0 + t/q_1$. Then $\|Tf\|_q \le M_0^{1-t}M_1^t\|f\|_p$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $I$ and $J$ are finite and carry counting measure.
The scalars are complex numbers, which the complex three lines theorem needs.
The exponents satisfy $p_i < \infty$ and $q_i > 1$, so the [conjugate exponents](c:holder-conjugate-exponents) $q_i'$ are finite.

conclusion: The $\ell^q$ norm of $Tf$ is at most $M_0^{1-t}M_1^t$ times the $\ell^p$ norm of $f$, for every $f$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the Hadamard three lines theorem for bounded functions on the strip. It is the analytic step 5, not Riesz-Thorin; mathlib has no Riesz-Thorin theorem.

proofs.name: Three lines theorem
proofs.slogan: Dualize the norm, build a holomorphic family in one variable, and bound it by the three lines theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. If $M_0$ or $M_1$ is 0, then $T = 0$ and the claim is trivial.

roles.why: Finite sums make the family $\Phi$ a finite sum of exponentials, so it is entire and bounded on the strip.
Complex phases and complex exponents allow a [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) family on the strip.
Finite conjugate exponents make the duality and the exponent maps defined.

steps.slogan: Write the $\ell^q$ norm as a supremum over unit vectors of the dual space.
steps.detail: For $1 < q < \infty$, $\|h\|_q = \sup\{|\sum_i h_i g_i| : \|g\|_{q'} = 1\}$. So it suffices to prove $|\sum_i (Tf)_i g_i| \le M_0^{1-t}M_1^t$ for $\|f\|_p = 1$ and $\|g\|_{q'} = 1$.

steps.slogan: Define exponent maps $a(z)$ and $b(z)$ on the strip with $a(t) = b(t) = 1$.
Build the entire function $\Phi(z)$ from $f$ and $g$ with phases and varying powers.
steps.detail: Put $f_z(j) = (f_j/|f_j|)|f_j|^{a(z)}$ and $g_z(i) = (g_i/|g_i|)|g_i|^{b(z)}$, with value 0 where the entry is 0, and $\Phi(z) = \sum_{i,j} T_{ij} f_z(j) g_z(i)$. Each term is a constant times an exponential of a linear function of $z$, so $\Phi$ is entire and bounded on $0 \le \mathrm{Re}\,z \le 1$. Also $\Phi(t) = \sum_i (Tf)_i g_i$.

steps.slogan: Bound $\Phi$ on the two edges of the strip by Holder and the operator norms.
steps.detail: On $\mathrm{Re}\,z = 0$, $|f_{iy}(j)| = |f_j|^{p/p_0}$, so $\|f_{iy}\|_{p_0} = 1$, and likewise $\|g_{iy}\|_{q_0'} = 1$. Holder and the definition of $M_0$ give $|\Phi(iy)| \le \|Tf_{iy}\|_{q_0}\|g_{iy}\|_{q_0'} \le M_0$. The same argument gives $|\Phi(1+iy)| \le M_1$.

steps.slogan: Apply Hadamard's three lines theorem to $\Phi$ on the strip.
steps.detail: The theorem gives $|\Phi(z)| \le M_0^{1-\mathrm{Re}\,z}M_1^{\mathrm{Re}\,z}$ for all $z$ in the strip. At $z = t$ this reads $|\Phi(t)| \le M_0^{1-t}M_1^t$.

steps.slogan: Take the supremum over $g$ and extend from unit vectors $f$ by homogeneity.
steps.detail: By step 3, $\Phi(t) = \sum_i (Tf)_i g_i$. The supremum over $g$ and the duality of step 1 give $\|Tf\|_q \le M_0^{1-t}M_1^t$ for $\|f\|_p = 1$. Homogeneity gives the general case.

concepts.c:matrix: The operator is a matrix, so every sum in the proof is finite.
concepts.c:operator-norm: The numbers $M_0$ and $M_1$ are the norms that the bound interpolates.
concepts.c:holder-conjugate-exponents: The conjugate exponents $q_i'$ define the dual norms in the duality and the edge bounds.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The three lines theorem needs a function holomorphic inside the strip.
